newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels move heavy guns to Tepelene.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels move heavy guns to Tepelene.

text.p: Former Albanian army officers have joined rebels in rolling heavy guns into this southern town while people searched empty shops for food.
A former army colonel who now controls the town placed a shell in a Chinese-made cannon in the town's main square and scanned a military map for targets to the north.
Tepelene, a mountain town of about 17,000 residents, is a main rebel stronghold in southern Albania along with the ports of Sarande and Vlore. Army or police are nowhere to be seen.
At the town's north and south entrances kids in paramilitary gear stop cars to check for "spiouni" -- secret police -- sent to collect information.
They fire warning shots but after checking documents they become friendly and treat the passengers to coffee next to a group of burned military cars.
Across the street, the police headquarters building is still smoking after protesters set it on fire on Monday.

"We are not gangsters as (President Sali) Berisha claims," the colonel, who asked not to be named, said. "The Albanian people took control and the minute Berisha resigns we will return the arms. If he sends troops, there will be bloodshed."

In Tepelene's abandoned army base the rebels move around ammunition and read instruction manuals for at least 50 cannons left behind when troops and police loyal to the government fled to the north on Tuesday.
Children wearing police caps and helmets play around ammunition cases and elderly women go through the base's trashed living quarters searching for blankets and food.

"Unfortunately a 12-year-old girl was killed on Wednesday when a Kalashnikov went off by mistake. We have now taken weapons away from kids under 16. The people took at least 5,000 guns from army depots around Tepelene," the colonel said.
He points to a warehouse with tonnes of dynamite guarded by about 10 masked men. A flock of sheep slowly makes its way through the barracks.

Inside the town about 30 women gather outside a bakery shop. Bread is expected to arrive from the government-controlled town of Gjirokaster, 30 km (18 miles) to the south for the first time in three days.
"There are plenty of bullets but no bread," said Melpo Karali, an elderly woman. "We have no money, the banks are looted, the shops are empty."

A dirt road leads into the mountains to a destroyed former top security prison where Fatos Nano, the head of the opposition Socialist Party, was held for three years before being flown to Tirana last Friday.
In cell number 5, where Nano was held, the walls are covered by postcards and letters sent from across Europe.
"My friend Fatos you are not alone. We are thinking of you and fight for your freedom," said a card sent from a London human rights group two weeks ago.
Several lieutenants of former Albanian leader Enver Hoxha had been held in cell 6 since 1991 after communism fell. They fled on Tuesday after the prison was left unguarded.
"We're trying to organise and put together a resistance. This is the only way we can face an attack from Berisha's forces," the colonel said.
Residents said they had seen an ageing Albanian air force MiG fighter on Wednesday evening firing into nearby mountains and at positions near the Vjose river running through the town.
Shops were empty, with residents systematically taking away anything left behind. A small crowd of men fought over who would use the town's sole working telephone. There is no electricity.
"God is against Albania," said Bejet Serjani. "He had the worst kind of kind of communism for 45 years and now all this mess."
